<reason>CON (A) built the clearer decision map and made PRO live inside it: PRO conceded the forbidden tier is handled by limits with "consent never a solvent," conceded a scoped file record is collected from a trainee who declines, and conceded that "soft favoritism exists wherever a right exists." That left consent governing only monitoring that PRO's own necessity test says "failed," which CON framed memorably as a price tag rather than a shield. PRO (B) fought back well—its "camera by another name" hit on CON's login face-check and trader-cam exceptions, plus the "no refuser to compare / necessity expands to fill the silence" reframe, kept a live route and made this competitive. But PRO's enforceable-floor answer was a near-shrug under direct pressure, and its defense of why consented-but-unnecessary monitoring should be permitted at all stayed thin. CON's two clipped speeches and its slightly strained labeling of a file ledger as "keystroke-derived" cost it some ground, keeping the margin clear but modest.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A2.1–A2.4: CON seized PRO's "if fraud detection needs a log, collect the log" and showed that under the motion's text the log is refusable while the kitchen camera is buyable, then argued consent's only remaining job is monitoring that fails PRO's own necessity test—a squeeze PRO never fully escaped despite its scoped-ledger distinction.</best_rebuttal>
